answer: Use set-alarm-state, which changes the operator state of an alarm and can store user data in the alarm itself. Syntax: set-alarm-state [state=]<value> [[acknowledge-text=]<value>] (all-alarms | [alarm-id-list=]<value>[,<value>]*). The state parameter is mandatory and takes operator-state values none, ack or close. Use all-alarms to set all currently raised alarms, or alarm-id-list to name specific alarms (from 1 up to 10 alarm ids). acknowledge-text is optional and inserts an acknowledge message, string length 0..256. Setting an alarm to its current state is accepted, with only the text being updated. Access Mode: Operational Mode. Example: set-alarm-state ack all-alarms acknowledge-text=example, or set-alarm-state ack 28872914984089790,17580406225060810165.

Yes. The statistics command clears the event counters (statistics) for the specified objects: clear [-f] statistics [target=]<value>[,<value>]*. Access Mode is Operational Mode. Flags: -h displays help, -f forces the command without confirmation. The target parameter is an instance-identifier naming the objects whose event counter statistics are cleared; multiple comma-separated targets are allowed. Scope is limited: currently the only supported object type is aaa-server, and AAA statistics are supported for TACACS+ servers but not for RADIUS servers. Example, clear all AAA servers: clear statistics aaa-server. Clear one server: clear statistics aaa-server-MyServer.

Use show log with the -n and -t flags: show [-n=<number>] [-t] log [<logname> [exclude=<exclude-column> ...]]. -n=x limits output to the last x log entries and -t switches from the default CSV output to an aligned table display. So for the last 5 security entries in table form: show -n=5 log security -t. Valid lognames include messages, linecard, shell-command, netconf-command, apps, cli-command, alarm, configuration, kernel, user, event, security and ztp. If the table becomes too wide, drop columns with exclude=<column> after the logname (use <tab> auto-complete to list removable columns). Output can also be piped, for example show log security | exclude john | include NETCONF. Access Mode: Operational mode, and Candidate Configuration mode for the show command only. Note the security log may not be cleared with clear log.

Yes, that is expected: console logging is off by default. The log-console object has an enabled attribute that switches console logging on and off, with values true or false and a default of false. Turn it on with: set log-console enabled true. Verify with show log-console. The other attribute is source-facilities, the list of syslog facilities used in this configuration, chosen from all, authentication, clock-daemon-15, clock-daemon-9, ftp-daemon, kernel, line-printer, local1 through local7, log-alert, log-audit, mail-system, network-news, ntp, security, syslog-internal, system-daemons, user-level and uucp. Syntax: set log-console [source-facilities <value>] [enabled <value>] / show log-console [source-facilities] [enabled]. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Add a log-console-facility-filter, a selector that filters messages by source facility and severity: add log-console-facility-filter-<name> [severity <value>] [compare-op <value>]. The <name> identifies a single syslog facility, or all of them if the value is 'all'. severity takes emergency (level 0), alert (1), critical (2), error (3), warning (4), notice (5), informational (6) or debug (7), and defaults to informational. compare-op controls how the comparison is made, with values equals, equals-or-higher or not-equals, default equals-or-higher. To keep informational messages off the console and show only serious ones: add log-console-facility-filter-all severity 'critical'. Use set to change an existing filter, show to view it and delete log-console-facility-filter-<name> to remove it. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Local history is bounded by two log-file attributes. max-file-size is the maximum file size before rotation in megabytes, uint8 range 1..30, default 30. number-of-files is the maximum number of log files retained, uint8 range 1..20, default 10: when rotating files because max-file-size is reached, the oldest files are discarded if the total number of files is greater than number-of-files. So by default the node keeps up to 10 files of up to 30 MB each before discarding. Set them with: set log-file-<name> number-of-files <value> max-file-size <value>. The log-file name is the file name without the .log extension, String length 0...128 characters. The default system log file cannot be edited or deleted; locally saved log files can be emptied with clear or removed with delete.

Yes. Create the local file restricted to the authentication facility, then optionally add a severity filter. Use add log-file-<name> [number-of-files <value>] [max-file-size <value>] [source-facilities <string>] [pattern-match <string>] [sensitive-data <value>], setting source-facilities to authentication (the facility used for authentication/authorization attempts messages, RFC facility 4); source-facilities defaults to all. For example: add log-file-authonly source-facilities authentication. To narrow severity, add log-file-facility-filter-<log-file-name>/<log-file-facility-filter-name> [severity <value>] [compare-op <value>], where the filter name identifies a single syslog facility or 'all'; severity defaults to informational and compare-op defaults to equals-or-higher. You can also constrain entries with pattern-match, a regex string of length 0..255.

Configure a log-server: add log-server-<name> address <IP address> ... port <value> transport <udp|tls|tcp>. transport is the transport protocol used when forwarding logs, with values tcp, udp and tls, and it defaults to udp, so you must specify transport tls explicitly. Unless you say otherwise, port defaults to 514 (range 1..65535) and message-format defaults to rfc5424 (the alternative is rfc3164). Other defaults: enabled true, message-coalescence true, source-facilities all, origin manual, sensitive-data none, destination-facility-override disabled, alarm-report-control allowed. address may be IPv4, IPv6 or a DNS domain name; name is a String of length 0...64. Example: add log-server-1 address '10.220.225.165' source-facilities local7.

Yes you can filter per collector, but the filter can only narrow, not widen. Use add log-server-facility-filter-<log-server-name>/<log-server-facility-filter-name> [severity <value>] [compare-op <value>]. The guide states this is a filter based on the source-facilities leaf-list and can only add a filter to the configured source facilities, so it cannot make the server send facilities that are not already in that log-server's source-facilities list. The filter name identifies a single syslog facility, or all of them if the value is 'all', chosen from kernel, user-level, mail-system, system-daemons, authentication, syslog-internal, line-printer, network-news, uucp, clock-daemon-9, security, ftp-daemon, ntp, log-audit, log-alert, clock-daemon-15, local0-local7 and all. severity defaults to informational and compare-op defaults to equals-or-higher (also equals, not-equals). Example: add log-server-facility-filter-server184/local2 severity debug.

Use the syslog remote-logging-switch flag: set syslog remote-logging-switch false. It is described as the flag to enable remote logging switch, and if false it disables all remote logging destinations; values are true or false with a default of true. This leaves the configured log-server entries in place. Related syslog attributes: log-relay (flag to enable remote logging from a shelf controller to a node controller, default false), source-address (default localhost), log-file-message-coalescence (default true), assignment-method (both, manual, dhcp, default both), niap-compliant-logging (default false), privacy-mode (default false), alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and label (string 0..256). Check the current setting with show syslog remote-logging-switch. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

The aaa-server page states that the maximum length of shared-secret is 64 characters, and any value more than 64 characters is denied with an error message. The parameter table lists shared-secret as the shared secret of the aaa server, type String (length 0...128), with default sharedkey; the shared secret is always displayed as * rather than in clear text. Set it with add aaa-server-<server-name> ... [shared-secret <value>] or set aaa-server-<server-name> [shared-secret <value>], and read it back with show aaa-server-<server-name> shared-secret. For reference, the server-name itself is a string of length 1...64. Access Mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode.

That is expected behaviour, not a bug. Under show aaa-statistics-<server-name> authentication-requests, the guide notes that for TACACS+ the default authentication protocol includes both PAP and CHAP, and the authentication requests counter tracks each retry and each authentication protocol attempted independently, so authentication requests may increase by 2 for each retry. The aaa-statistics command applies only to AAA servers that use the TACACS+ protocol. Available counters are connection-failures (failures due to unavailable servers and timeouts), authentication-requests, authentication-rejects, authorization-requests, authorization-rejects and accounting-requests, all integers. Example: show aaa-statistics-tacacs_server1. You can reset the counters with clear statistics aaa-server-<name>.

If you omit action, the ACE drops matching packets: the action parameter, the action taken by the filter, has values drop, accept and reject with a default of drop. Pre-condition: an ACL must be in place before an ACE can be added, and at least one of Source IP, Destination IP, L4 ports, TTL or protocol must be provided. Limits: the sequence-id range is 1-100 for AUX and DCN-B interfaces and 1-256 for the DCN-A interface, and it is recommended to use multiples of 5 so rules can be inserted later. A maximum of 16 ACEs can be created on an ACL if both upper-port and lower-port values are specified; adding a seventeenth such ACE returns an error. Other defaults: direction input, logging-action false, protocol any, ttl 255, source/destination lower and upper port 0. Example: add ace-TrafficV6/100 action drop source-ip-address 2420::5.

An ACL is bound to one management interface at creation: add acl-<name> type <value> interface <value> [admin-state <value>]. The available interfaces are 1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-B, DCN-2 and DCN-2-B (use add acl-name interface ? to list them). Yes, IPv6 is handled: the type parameter indicates the top-level type of ACL, that is which fields from the associated IPv4 or IPv6 headers the ACL matches on, with values IPv4 and IPv6, and it is mandatory on add. name is a string of length 0...30 and admin-state takes lock, maintenance or unlock, default unlock. An ACL can have one or more ACEs. Note: an ACL can be added on the DCN-B interface when the DCN is operating in active-active configuration. Example: add acl-AuxV4traffic interface 1-AUX-2 type ipv4.

Yes: show access-control-list. It is a show-only command used to display the access control list, it takes no parameters, and its Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. To work with individual lists and their entries instead, use the acl commands (add/set/show/delete acl-<name>, with type, interface, admin-state, oper-state and avail-state) and the ace commands (add/set/show/delete ace-<name>/<sequence-id>) for each access control entry within an ACL.

Create an access-rule-list bound to that group, then add a deny rule for the path. First: add access-rule-list-<name> [user-group <value>] [sequence-id <value>] [description <value>], for example add access-rule-list-A user-group XY. Then: add access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name> action <value> [sequence-id <value>] [module-name <value>] [path <value>] [attribute <value>] [attribute-value <value>] [operation <value>] [description <value>]. action is mandatory whenever a rule is created and takes permit or deny. path is the target object, an XPath of a YANG data node, notification, RPC or descendant, or an external command, max length 255, default *. operation is a bits value from create, read, update, delete and execute, default * (all). Example, deny card creation: add access-rule-1/rule path /ne/equipment/card operation create action deny. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists.

Order is by sequence-id: the access-rule-list is processed in order as given by the sequence-id parameter, and lower number ids are processed first, so the lowest sequence-id wins first. sequence-id is a uint16 and can be changed over the lifetime of the list to re-sort entries; if you do not provide it, it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, that is the entry goes to the end of the list. The same sequence-id rule applies to individual access-rules within a list. To say which groups a list applies to, use the user-group parameter: add access-rule-list-<name> [user-group <value>] [sequence-id <value>] [description <value>]. user-group is a leaf-list of user-group names or '*', defaulting to '*' as a match-all meaning the list applies to all existing user-groups; a maximum of 20 user-groups can be referenced. Example: add access-rule-list-A user-group XY.

Despite the generic name, auth-key is OSPF-specific: it configures the pre-shared key for OSPFv3 IPsec integrity protection. The AID is scoped entirely by OSPF: add auth-key-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi> key <value> [type <value>], with matching set, show and delete forms. instance-id is the OSPF instance ID, a number in range 0..255; ospf-area-id is the OSPF Router Area ID (string); ospf-if-name is a reference to the interface in the OSPF area; and spi is a unique security parameter index for this SA, a number in range 256..4294967295. key is a string of length 8..128, and type indicates whether the integrity key is ASCII or hexadecimal encoded, values ascii or hex. Example: add auth-key-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 key abcdefgh12345678. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Set the global authorization mode to rules-only: set authorization mode rules-only. mode selects which kind of authorization rules are used, with values static-only (only system defined static authorization rules), static+rules (both user and system defined access-rules, the system tries a user configured access-rule first and falls back to system rules) and rules-only (only user defined access-rules; if no rule matches, the global defaults are used). The default is static+rules. In rules-only mode the fallbacks are read-default, write-default and exec-default, each permit or deny and only configurable when mode = rules-only; their defaults are read-default permit, write-default deny, exec-default permit. To deny everything the rules do not cover, set all three to deny, for example set authorization write-default deny. show authorization also reports denied-operations, denied-data-writes and denied-notifications counters since the last restart.

Every user changes their own password with the password command: password [old-password=<old-password>] [new-password=<new-password>]. Both the current/old password and the new password are required, and this is supported only for local users. A password may contain up to 200 characters. Input can be inline, as normal parameters that are not hidden from view and are usable in scripts, or interactive, where the passwords are prompted for and not echoed and the new one must be typed twice; interactive input can be cancelled with Ctrl+C. Inline, special characters \"' must be escaped with \\ and #?|; must be enclosed in quotes. Example: password old-password=Infinera4u! new-password=Infinera4us!. To reset another user's password as an admin, use set user-<username> force-password-change true, which forces the user to change their password on next login. Access Mode for password: Operational mode.

Use show security. It is the command that shows the top level security container, it takes no parameters, and its Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show security. For the individual settings underneath it, use show security-policies for the security policy flags (secure-mode, strict-password-check, minimum-password-length, ssh and TLS algorithm lists, and so on), show access-control-list for ACLs, and show user-group, show user or show user-data for the user side.

Minimum password length is governed by minimum-password-length under security-policies: a configurable minimum length for user passwords, number in range 1..200, default 8; the length is verified against this policy whenever a password is changed. strict-password-check (true/false, default true) additionally enforces a minimum length of 8 characters, at least one lower case letter (a-z), at least one upper case letter (A-Z), at least one number (0-9), at least one symbol, and that the user name cannot be part of the password; if disabled, only a minimum length of 1 character applies. For password reuse, enforce-password-history-check (true/false, default true) ensures a new password cannot match any of the previous 5 passwords, and password-history-size sets the number of passwords stored for reuse checking, number in range 1..200, default 5. Both history and strictness policies affect only newly defined passwords once enabled.

Lockout is per user, on the user object. max-invalid-login is the maximum number of consecutive invalid login attempts before an account is suspended (locked out), a number in range 0-255 with a default of 5. suspension-time is the duration of UID suspension following consecutive invalid login attempts, in minutes, range 0 - 1440, default 5 minutes. So by default 5 failed logins lock the account for 5 minutes. Set them with add user-<user-name> [max-invalid-login <value>] [suspension-time <value>] or the equivalent set. show user-<user-name> reports failed-logins, the number of previous failed logins, which resets to zero upon a successful login, and user-status, where the value lockout means the account is locked out due to unsuccessful login attempts. Lockout can also be turned off globally with the security-policies disable-user-lockout attribute.

user-data is a show-only command: show user-data. The guide states the commands in that section are used to show the user-data, its Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, and its Command Parameters section is None, so it takes no arguments and no per-attribute selectors. For per-user attributes such as user-group, max-invalid-login, suspension-time, timeout, password-aging-interval, password-expiration-date, user-status, last-login-date, failed-logins and user-aaa-type, use show user-<user-name> instead.

Use add user-group-<name> [description <value>]. Each user is associated with a list of groups and derives its permissions from them. name is the name of the group, a String of 1...64 characters, and description is a long description of the user group, a String of 1...128 characters. The matching commands are set user-group-<name> [description <value>], show user-group-<name> [description] and delete user-group-<name>. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add user-group-XY, then delete user-group-XY to remove it. show user-group lists the built-in groups: EA Encryption Administrator, MA Monitoring Access, NA Network Administrator, NE Network Engineer, PR Provisioning, SA Security Administrator and TT Turn-up and Test. Assign groups to a user with add user-<user-name> user-group <value>, and reference groups from an access-rule-list with its user-group parameter.
